Broken Chord

GeometryCirclesTriangles
Game: This is a picture to explore: move the corners of a triangle on a circle and watch where a line from the circle cuts the bent path from A to C to B.
How to play: Drag A, B or C with a mouse or finger, or focus a point and use the arrow keys. Press Show hint to see the proof lines, or Check the claim to read the result.
Look for the math

The line from P lands on the longest side, yet the piece it cuts off equals the other two pieces of the bent path put together. Drag the corners about: it keeps happening. That is the Broken Chord Theorem, credited to Archimedes.

The picture

A, B and C lie on the circumcircle of their triangle. P is the midpoint of the arc ACB: of the two places where the perpendicular bisector of chord AB meets the circle, it is the one on the same side of AB as C. The line from P is dropped onto the longer of AC and BC, and its foot is M. The broken line is the path A–C–B along the two sides of the triangle.

Adding the point F

Suppose AC is the longer side. Extend it past C to F so that CF = BC. Then BCF is an isosceles triangle: its base angles at B and F are equal, so the outside angle ACB at C is twice the angle at F. Angles ACB and APB stand on the same chord AB, so they are equal too, and angle APB = 2 × angle AFB.

Why P is the centre

In triangle ABF, the angle at F is an inscribed angle on chord AB. The angle at P is twice as large, so P is the centre of the circle through A, B and F: press Show hint to see that circle. A line from the centre of a circle perpendicular to a chord cuts the chord in half, hence

AM = MF = MC + CF = MC + BC.

The logic test checks this equality and its supporting facts at 204 positions, and checks that the applet's own circumcircle, P, M and F agree with this code at every one of them.

The other side and the edge cases

The applet compares AC with BC and uses the longer one. If BC wins, the foot M lies on BC and the claim reads BM = MC + AC instead; the test covers that mirror case too. When A, B and C are almost in a straight line the circumcircle has no centre, and both the applet and this page draw nothing until you spread them out.

Try dragging C across the middle: watch M jump to the other side as AC and BC swap, and the equality change from AM = MC + BC to BM = MC + AC.
